enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable: Qualitative legal-documentary and theoretical study with no longitudinal participant sample or municipal cohort subject to follow-up loss.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern / Weak: Although contextual moderators (municipal size, regional associative culture, local administration political projects and technical complexity) are noted conceptually, there is no empirical comparator or analytical strategy to separate statutory design effects from socio-political confounding.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-weak: Core Brazilian federal sanitation and health participation instruments (1988 Federal Constitution, Law 8.142/1990, Law 11.445/2007, Decree 7.217/2010, 2006 Ministry of Cities PMSB guide and 2012 FUNASA PMSB Terms of Reference) and the consultative-versus-deliberative council distinction are accurately identified at a macro level, but specific statutory articles are omitted in the text, Table 1 duplicates entries, and the reference list imprecisely cites Articles 5, 6 and 144 of the Constitution.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern / Weak: No empirical measurement instruments, documentary coding protocol or standardized extraction criteria are reported; claims regarding council dynamics rely on narrative interpretation of secondary literature (largely on Municipal Health Councils) rather than direct empirical measurement of sanitation forums.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / No empirical measurement: Neither social control effectiveness nor water and sanitation service or health outcomes are empirically operationalized or measured; outcomes are addressed solely in conceptual and normative terms.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some-to-high concern / Weak: No study protocol, systematic document inventory or structured extraction matrix is reported, and findings reflect selective narrative synthesis aligned with the authors' theoretical framework without systematic reporting of disconfirming evidence.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Weak: Official documents (Table 1) and secondary studies were purposively selected using broad keywords without reporting databases searched, date ranges, eligible document universes or inclusion/exclusion criteria, creating substantial risk of selective citation.

domain_ratings.justification: The authors accurately identify key federal statutes and administrative guidance governing social control in Brazilian basic sanitation and public health—Law 11.445 of 5 January 2007 (PNSB), Decree 7.217 of 21 June 2010, Law 8.142 of 28 December 1990 (SUS community participation), the 2006 Ministry of Cities PMSB guide and the 2012 FUNASA PMSB Terms of Reference—and correctly contrast consultative sanitation councils under Law 11.445/2007 with deliberative health councils under Law 8.142/1990. However, statutory provisions are summarized broadly without article-level precision, Table 1 repeats the Ministry of Cities Environmental Sanitation Policy and Plan entry, and the reference list cites Articles 5, 6 and 144 (public security) of the 1988 Constitution rather than specific health, urban or participatory articles.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1-6, 10-11 (Introduction; Table 1; Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; References)

domain_ratings.justification: The institutional analysis is clearly bounded to Brazil's federal constitutional and statutory framework (1988 Constitution, PNSB under Law 11.445/2007, FUNASA and Ministry of Cities/SNSA guidelines) and its municipal implementation interface via Basic Sanitation Municipal Plans (PMSBs) and municipal councils, although subnational variation across Brazilian municipalities is addressed only conceptually through secondary literature.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1-7 (Introduction; Table 1; Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation)

domain_ratings.justification: The institutional governance mechanism of interest—formalized popular participation and social control arenas in sanitation, specifically consultative councils under Law 11.445/2007 and participatory PMSB planning processes contrasted with deliberative SUS health councils—is clearly conceptualized, though not operationalized into empirical variables.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1-7 (Introduction; Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation)

domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes such as effective social control, citizenship development, community empowerment, sustainability of sanitation infrastructure and health promotion are framed purely as abstract theoretical and normative constructs without operational definitions or measurable empirical indicators.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2, 4-10 (Introduction; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation; Final considerations)

domain_ratings.justification: While the authors state that documental research used four broad keywords (social control, popular participation, social participation and sanitation) and list federal documents in Table 1, they provide no information on bibliographic or legislative repositories searched, search dates, universe of candidate federal or municipal documents, or eligibility criteria.

Official policy documents in Table 1 (including duplicated entries) and secondary academic studies (drawn heavily from municipal health council case studies) were purposively assembled to illustrate theoretical arguments without any documented screening workflow or safeguards against selective inclusion.

The study employs no empirical measurement tools, structured documentary extraction rubrics or empirical indicators of council functioning or PMSB implementation; diagnoses of executive dominance and technification of discourse rest on qualitative narrative synthesis of prior literature.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-9 (Table 1; Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation)

domain_ratings.justification: No empirical design or counterfactual comparison is used to identify causal effects of Law 11.445/2007's consultative council structure or PMSB participatory mandates on citizen participation or sanitation service outcomes; causal inferences are purely theoretical and interpretive.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-10 (Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation; Final considerations)

domain_ratings.justification: Although the text acknowledges contextual influences such as municipal size, local civil society organization, local executive political agendas and technical complexity, there is no empirical strategy to control or account for these confounders when attributing participation deficits to institutional design.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 4, 6-9 (Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation)

domain_ratings.justification: The article offers substantive contextualization of Brazil's post-1988 participatory governance architecture, detailing the roles of FUNASA and the Ministry of Cities/SNSA in PMSB funding and guidelines, sectoral policy fragmentation, technocratic dominance over user representatives in municipal councils and the contradictions of state-sponsored social control.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1, 3-9 (Introduction; Social control of public policies; Social control strategies in sanitation; Strengthening social participation in sanitation)

domain_ratings.justification: Although the cited statutes and federal guides are publicly identifiable (despite duplicate bibliography lines and dated URLs in the reference list), the lack of search parameters, selection rules and analytical procedures prevents independent replication of the documentary and literature synthesis.
Table 1 maps official documents onto three broad analytical themes, but no coding framework, textual extraction sheet or qualitative content-analysis procedure is described.

The authors apply explicit normative and theoretical commitments (including Raymundo Faoro's critique of Brazilian political patronage and participatory democracy theory) without reflecting on researcher positionality or how those commitments shaped source selection and interpretation.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: S425 (Silva & Naval, 2015) is a qualitative legal-institutional documentary study and theoretical policy analysis examining social control and popular participation mechanisms in Brazilian basic sanitation governance. Drawing on a small set of federal legal and administrative texts tabulated in Table 1 (1988 Federal Constitution, Law 8.142/1990 on SUS health councils, Law 11.445/2007 establishing the National Policy for Basic Sanitation [PNSB], Decree 7.217/2010, and FUNASA and Ministry of Cities guidelines for Basic Sanitation Municipal Plans [PMSBs]) alongside secondary Brazilian social science literature and Raymundo Faoro's political theory, the authors contrast consultative sanitation councils under Law 11.445/2007 with deliberative health councils under Law 8.142/1990 and diagnose institutional barriers such as executive dominance, policy fragmentation, lack of citizenship education and technification of council discourse. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment, with no numeric composite score), the study demonstrates adequate jurisdictional specificity, conceptual framing of the participatory governance exposure, institutional contextualization and macro-level identification of federal statutes (notwithstanding omitted statutory article numbers, duplicated entries in Table 1 and an imprecise citation to Constitutional Articles 5, 6 and 144 in the bibliography). However, empirical and methodological rigor is weak: no primary empirical data were collected on sanitation councils or municipal sanitation outcomes, no search strategy or inclusion criteria govern document or literature selection, no coding or measurement protocol is reported, and no empirical causal identification or confounding control is attempted.
raw_response.overall_rating: Weak empirical rigor / High methodological concern (structured non-validated judgment; no composite score)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Qualitative legal-institutional documentary analysis and theoretical policy essay on Brazilian basic sanitation governance (analyzing federal constitutional/statutory provisions and administrative PMSB guidelines alongside narrative secondary literature, with no primary field data or systematic review protocol)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methods and documentary corpus in Introduction and Table 1 (PDF pp. 1-2); comparative legal-institutional discussion in 'Social control of public policies' (PDF pp. 3-4), 'Social control strategies in sanitation' (PDF pp. 4-7) and 'Strengthening social participation in sanitation' (PDF pp. 7-9); normative synthesis in 'Final considerations' (PDF pp. 9-10); legal/bibliographic citations in 'References' (PDF pp. 10-13) and 'Abstract' (PDF p. 15).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper conducts a qualitative documentary analysis of Brazilian federal constitutional, statutory (Law 8.142/1990; Law 11.445/2007; Decree 7.217/2010) and administrative sanitation planning instruments (Table 1: FUNASA and Ministry of Cities PMSB guidelines) combined with theoretical/narrative synthesis of secondary literature. It collects no primary human-participant or field data (making CASP Qualitative's recruitment, participant-relationship and ethics items ill-suited), employs no quantitative sample or comparator (ruling out RoB 2, ROBINS-I, JBI and MMAT) and has no systematic review protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2 per protocol rules). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly evaluates its legal-documentary accuracy, institutional contextualization and empirical/methodological limitations.
